learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of passwords and authentication data and identify when it is appropriate in a Java program.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study passwords and authentication data with a short explanation, an original visual map, a Java example, and a check you can perform yourself. Focus on the relationship between the rule and the behavior rather than memorizing isolated syntax.
content.why_it_matters: This concept matters because it helps you enforce security policy at trust boundaries and use vetted platform primitives. In this lesson, focus on password hashing concepts and use a minimal example to check what the rule actually guarantees.

items.title: Salt and work factors
items.text: Security depends on trust boundaries and explicit policy, not on a value’s Java type. Validate untrusted inputs, use standard cryptography and secure defaults, and keep secrets out of logs and source control. Apply that reasoning specifically to salt and work factors and confirm the result with the example or a targeted test.

items.title: Avoiding plaintext passwords and reversible storage
items.text: Primitive variables store values of the eight primitive types. Choose a type that represents the domain and range required; use exact decimal arithmetic for monetary values when appropriate.

items.title: Delegating authentication to trusted systems when appropriate
items.text: Use Path and Files for modern file operations, choose byte or character APIs based on the data, and close resources reliably. Parse external files defensively because their contents may be incomplete or malformed.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Normalize and validate at a clear boundary, with explicit rules for accepted values. For ordinary Java SE examples, use JDK 25, save a complete class as Main.java, and run `javac Main.java` followed by `java Main`. CodeLeaf does not execute Java in the browser; use a local JDK for these examples. Preview-only and configuration-file examples have their own version or filename notes.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original example, remove any temporary output files it created, and rerun the baseline case. Do not leave credentials, generated private data, or large test files in the project directory.

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Keep one clear hypothesis per experiment. Check the version, read the error message, test boundaries, and record what evidence supports your conclusion.

content.task: Try it yourself: apply the safe-coding principle in passwords and authentication data to synthetic data. Document the trust boundary, the expected rejection behavior, and the information that must never be logged.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating input or configuration as trusted just because it is typed as a Java String.
common_mistakes.why: Types describe representation; they do not prove that input meets the application policy.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate at trust boundaries, keep secrets out of logs, and reject invalid input explicitly.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing only a single happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Boundary values and failures often reveal assumptions hidden by the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add an empty, boundary, or invalid case and state the expected behavior before running it.

common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify the actual cause of a different result.
common_mistakes.fix: Change one factor at a time and keep a short record of observed behavior.
